fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Speaking more broadly, formal verification in proof assistants is interesting because in the robustly mathematical setting provided by proof assistants, one can state and prove arbitrary properties.
This may be a blessing and a curse. Much like with programming languages, being able to state and do arbitrary things is not always an advantage.
Due to the extreme flexibility, formal counterparts of informal specifications can vary widely without an obvious way to compare them or evaluate them for correctness or practical utility (for more on this see the introduction to my PhD thesis).

In my PhD and my subsequent writing (e.g. this paper or my research statement), I have argued that the robustly mathematical setting of proof assistants offers us an opportunity for unmatched rigor, but we must draw on mathematical practice and tradition and use them in a more sophisticated way than we are using them now. There is much to be learned from the ongoing work in the formalization of mathematics and formal specification and verification in proof assistants more broadly, from theoretical and practical perspectives.

Most of my formal research work is in formal specification and verification, especially in proof assistants like Lean, Rocq, and the like.
During my PhD and in the years after a lot of time thinking about smart contract design, specification, and verification.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Smart Contract Design, Specification, and Verification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Smart contracts are interesting from the perspective of formal specification and verification because:

html:ol.html:li: they are typically small in size, with a deterministic and well-defined execution environment, making them feasible to formally reason about in a short time frame, and
they often manage huge sums of money (so the incentives line up).

The reason the rest of this corpus is organised the way it is. The verified zkEVM effort runs three tracks — the zkVM constraints, the EVM semantics, and the cryptography — and ArkLib and CompPoly are the cryptography track.

These pages stay closer to the code than the rest of the corpus, which also makes them the ones most likely to go stale. Related: protocol snarkification, computable specifications, formal verification in proof assistants.
A modular library of formally verified arguments of knowledge in Lean, organised around interactive oracle reductions rather than around individual protocols.

Which developments are blocked on CompPoly.

Computable polynomials and finite fields in Lean: an executable mirror of the Mathlib definitions, with transfer theorems so proofs can be done on the noncomputable side. The case for computable specifications is made elsewhere; this page is about the artefact.

The representations chosen, and which operations each makes cheap. See univariate and multilinear polynomials.

fr:title.text: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The statement at the top of the whole effort, written out honestly: which theorems compose, and which links in the chain are assumptions rather than proofs. It is the claim the whole effort will be judged on, and its general form is the issue of incorrect specification: a machine-checked proof is only ever as good as the statement it proves.

Questions this page should answer:
The chain: ISA specification, constraint system, arithmetisation soundness, IOP soundness, commitment security, Fiat–Shamir, recursion, extracted implementation.
Which links are proved today, which are stated, and which are not formalised at all.
The irreducible assumptions: hash security, conjectured proximity bounds, the compiler, the hardware.
Whether "verified" should mean the composed end-to-end theorem, or a set of component theorems with audited seams.
The 2027 target the project set, and what would have to be true for it to be met.
Sources: verified-zkevm.org, Verified-zkEVM overview.

I am interested, broadly speaking, in formal proposition and proof. From a high level, what tends to catch my attention is the nuance of going from an intuitive, abstract idea into something formal—whether it's a formal specification of a program, a formalized theorem statement, or even something simply written out as a program.

During my PhD this manifested as written work focused on the problem of (correctly) specifying and formally verifying financial smart contracts. But I continue to be interested in software verification more broadly, the ongoing work to formalize mathematics, and other developments in using proof assistants in production.
I recently started work on formally verifying all things zero-knowledge on the Ethereum protocol, so my interests are broadening but are still rooted in the same topics.

Newest first:
zkVMs and SNARKs. A systematic study of the cryptography and machine architecture these systems are built from, topic by topic: arithmetisation, commitment schemes, low-degree testing from FRI to WHIR, zkVMs themselves, and formalising the stack in Lean. August 2026.
LC3 in Lean. A small virtual machine and its semantics in Lean, with the ISA-level details and the proofs of correctness written up separately. March 2026.
CompPoly and Computable Specifications. Why an executable specification is a stronger specification, and how that connects to metaspecifications in cryptography. March 2026.
Protocol Snarkification. Ongoing work to integrate zero knowledge proofs into every layer of the Ethereum protocol. December 2025.
Formal Specification and Verification. Smart contract specification and verification, and formal verification in proof assistants more broadly. August 2025.
Type Theory and Formal Proof. Proof assistants, some preliminary work in HoTT, and the formalization of mathematics in Lean. August 2025.
There has been a great deal of community-driven work in the formalization of mathematics in Lean, Rocq, Isabelle/HOL, and Agda.

Formal verification is the practice of mathematically proving code to be correct with regards to a specification (a formal description). This can be done in many ways, most interestingly (in my opinion) within interactive theorem provers like Lean or Rocq.
Formal proposition and proof, especially in Lean and Rocq, catch my attention from various angles. This is my most recent research statement as a PDF. (Last updated 09/2025.)

fr:title.text: The Background to my PhD Thesis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Background to my PhD Thesis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From October 2019 until December 2023, I was a PhD student at the University of Cambridge. I started my PhD trying to look at the Adam's Spectral Sequence in HoTT (ambitious, by what I'm given to understand), but life and covid lockdowns happened. I ended up pivoting into interactive theorem proving, thinking about financial smart contracts and their specifications.

The main question that haunted me during my PhD was this: We can prove software correct with regards to a specification, but how does one know that a specification is correct? What could a notion of "correctness" even look like for software specifications?

What followed was a prolonged meditation on the nature of the process of going from ideas and intuition into concrete implementation. My research was mostly an exploration on the formal tools used to write formal specifications. I was particularly fascinated by the use of interactive theorem provers (ITPs)—Rocq, Lean, Isabelle/HOL and the like—to specify smart contracts because of their extreme flexibility and versatility. You can state and prove anything in these, which can be thrilling but also provides a huge amount of flexibility.

At the same time, the formalization of mathematics (in Lean) was beginning to catch my attention. The computer lab at the time had a weekly seminar on the formalization of mathematics, which I could attend when it didn't conflict with my commitments with Clare choir. While I knew I was not interested in actually doing the formalization myself, I was unquestionably drawn into the research of those that were—in particular, the observations they made about the intricacies of going from pen-and-paper proofs to formal proofs.

Mathematicians were finding small, nuanced, and implicit assumptions made and expressed intuitively through notation and definitions that all mathematicians seemed to understand and get, but that had to be both discovered and made explicit during the process of formalization. I really started to learn the role of intuition that a mathematician undergoes when they codify a new mathematical concept into a formal definition—both in the realm of pen-and-paper mathematics as well as in the realm of formal proof.

It was during this time that I started to experiment with formal definitions and structures that are common to mathematics, and highly useful for mathematical definitions, for the specification and verification of smart contracts. The structures and definitions I chose, mostly from very basic category theory, play a heavy role in modern theories of computation and programming languages but do not feature in specifications themselves (e.g. from a behavioral perspective).

fr:title.text: The Main Contributions of my PhD Thesis

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Main Contributions of my PhD Thesis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: My PhD thesis proposes two different ways of handling the problem of a specification's correctness. Both draw heavily on the theoretically robust nature of proof assistants.

The first is through what I would informally call the "meta work," where the specification itself is treated like a mathematical object to study and prove correctness, like the software we're trying to prove correct. This uses prose and specification to articulate desired behaviors of a smart contract that are already easy to define, e.g. desirable economic or game-theoretic properties.

The second is through the use of abstract tools that approximate the desired behavior. My first motivating example is that of a smart contract upgrade. When upgrading any software, intuitively we understand an updated version as incrementally different from a previous version—we're adding feature X, Y, and Z, fixing bugs, removing outdated functionality. All of this frames conversation and understanding of the new software in terms of the old. Why not then apply that to the formal specification?

I introduced the notion of a contract morphism, or a formal structural relationship between two contracts that could be used in specification. The term "morphism" is category-theoretic, and is a general mathematical way of establishing a relationship between two objects. Once this formal relationship is established, proofs of one contract can be transported over that relationship to another contract. If the morphism is invertible, then the formal relationship establishes an equivalence of contracts, which could be useful e.g. for proving optimized code correct with regards to a reference implementation. The morphism allows one to use a contract as a specification, something which can be far more intuitive than using prose.
All of this is encapsulated fairly well in the slides of this talk.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Paper Abstract: Poorly specified smart contracts can be vulnerable to attacks on faulty design. Formal methods are currently unable to address these vulnerabilities because they are not vulnerabilities of incorrect code, but of incorrect specification. We are thus in need of a paradigm shift in how we specify and verify smart contracts which allows for a rigorous and accurate notion of a contract specification’s correctness. We submit that correctness includes appropriate cryptoeconomic behaviors, which are generally out of scope of a contract’s specification. We advocate for an approach to contract specification consisting of contract axiomatization and metaspecification, and illustrate with an example.
